evidence.claim: highlights its volcanic geology, wild rivers, pastoral valleys and Barlow Road history.
evidence.quote: On this byway volcanoes once erupted and mammoth floods scoured deep gorges. Discover geologic wonders, waterfalls, temperate rain forests and wild rivers. Explore pastoral valleys with farm-fresh produce. Experience the formidable last leg of the Oregon Trail, the Barlow Road.

evidence.claim: Sam Barlow and Philip Foster built the Barlow Road in 1846, opening an overland wagon crossing of the Cascades to the Willamette Valley.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1846 by Sam Barlow and Philip Foster, with authorization of the Provisional Legislature of Oregon, and served as the last overland segment of the Oregon Trail. Its construction allowed covered wagons to cross the Cascade Range and reach the Willamette Valley

evidence.claim: Before that road opened, arrivals from the east at The Dalles had faced a river journey down the Columbia.
evidence.quote: Before the opening of the Barlow Road, pioneers traveling by land from the east followed the Oregon Trail to Wascopam Mission (now The Dalles) and floated down the Columbia River to Fort Vancouver

evidence.claim: The Mount Hood Highway later displaced much of the wagon road; part of the historic route joined the scenic byway in 2005.
evidence.quote: The road was rendered largely irrelevant in the early 1900s by the construction of the Mount Hood Highway.

evidence.claim: part of the historic route joined the scenic byway in 2005.
evidence.quote: In 2005, part of it was incorporated into the Mount Hood Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Starting at Troutdale, the byway follows local streets toward Sandy, then climbs on US 26 toward Government Camp.
evidence.quote: From Troutdale, the Mount Hood Scenic Byway starts at the end of the Historic Columbia River Highway where the Troutdale Bridge crosses the Sandy River.

evidence.claim: Laurel Hill lies west of Government Camp; the Timberline Lodge spur leaves just east of town.
evidence.quote: A roadside marker and trail at Laurel Hill (just west of Government Camp)

evidence.claim: Back on the main route, OR 35 winds over Bennett Pass and along the mountain’s eastern side before descending into the Hood River Valley.
evidence.quote: Route 35 winds over Bennett Pass and around the eastern side of Mount Hood, and descends into the Hood River Valley.

evidence.claim: Pear, cherry and apple orchards mark the valley on the way to Hood River.
evidence.quote: Pear, cherry and apple trees — and, increasingly, vineyards — checkerboard the valley

evidence.claim: the Timberline Lodge spur leaves just east of town.
evidence.quote: The Byway follows a spur just east of Government Camp to Timberline Lodge.

evidence.claim: Laurel Hill put wagon brakes to a severe test on the Barlow Road.
evidence.quote: It was one of the steepest descents of any on the Oregon Trail.

evidence.claim: Travelers dragged trees behind their wagons to slow the descent, or lowered them with ropes and chains.
evidence.quote: had to either drag trees behind their wagons for braking or winch using ropes or chains.

evidence.claim: They considered this the worst part of the Oregon Trail.
evidence.quote: Travelers considered it the worst part of the entire Oregon Trail

evidence.claim: Even the name records a mistake: travelers took the rhododendrons here for laurels.
evidence.quote: The name came from travelers mistaking rhododendrons as laurels.

evidence.claim: A historical marker on US 26 and a short trail identify the place now.
evidence.quote: The location is marked today by a historical marker on U.S. Route 26 in Oregon and a short hiking trail

evidence.claim: The trail reaches the top and bottom of a wagon chute, as well as the later Mt. Hood Loop Highway.
evidence.quote: to the top and bottom of one of the chutes the wagons used as well as the later Mt. Hood Loop Highway.

evidence.claim: Government Camp takes its name from wagons that did not finish their journey.
evidence.quote: Government Camp was given its name by settlers traveling the Barlow Road, who discovered several wagons abandoned there by the Regiment of Mounted Riflemen.

evidence.claim: Settlers on the Barlow Road found wagons abandoned by the Regiment of Mounted Riflemen; a sign outside the post office dates the naming to 1849.
evidence.quote: A sign in front of the town's post office states, "Formerly a camp on the old Barlow Road, the village was named in 1849 when U.S Cavalry troops were forced to abandon wagons and supplies here."

evidence.claim: The community sits on US 26 near its junction with OR 35 and serves as a gateway to Timberline Lodge and Mount Hood Skibowl.
evidence.quote: The community is located within the Mount Hood Corridor on U.S. Route 26 (the Mount Hood Highway), near its intersection with Oregon Route 35

evidence.claim: Travel Oregon describes a summer and winter recreation hub whose story is presented at the Mt. Hood Cultural Center & Museum.
evidence.quote: Government Camp , a busy recreational and cultural hub in the summer and winter, depicted at the Mt. Hood Cultural Center & Museum .

evidence.claim: serves as a gateway to Timberline Lodge and Mount Hood Skibowl.
evidence.quote: It is the gateway to several ski resorts, with the most popular being Timberline Lodge and Mount Hood Skibowl.

evidence.claim: A twisting six-mile road climbs from Government Camp to Timberline Lodge at 6,000 feet.
evidence.quote: a twisting 6-mile/9.6- kilometer road leads steeply uphill to the majestic Timberline Lodge

evidence.claim: The Works Progress Administration built the lodge from 1936 to 1938, with local artisans making its furnishings during the Great Depression.
evidence.quote: Constructed from 1936 to 1938 by the Works Progress Administration, it was built and furnished by local artisans during the Great Depression.

evidence.claim: Reused materials became part of the craft: old Civilian Conservation Corps blankets supplied hooked rugs, and discarded cedar utility poles became carved newel posts.
evidence.quote: Hooked rugs were made from strips of old Civilian Conservation Corps camp blankets. Discarded cedar utility poles became newel-posts with their crowns hand-carved into birds, bears, and seals.

evidence.claim: Local boulders form the heavy ground-floor masonry, with timber above.
evidence.quote: The ground-level exterior walls are heavy rubble masonry, using boulders from the immediate area, and heavy timber is used from the first floor up.

evidence.claim: The National Historic Landmark’s exterior also served as the Overlook Hotel in The Shining.
evidence.quote: It is notable in film for serving as the exterior of the Overlook Hotel in The Shining (1980).

evidence.claim: Heavy rubble masonry forms the ground-floor walls, with timber above.
evidence.quote: The ground-level exterior walls are heavy rubble masonry, using boulders from the immediate area, and heavy timber is used from the first floor up.

evidence.claim: Timberline Lodge at 6,000 feet.
evidence.quote: The National Historic Landmark sits at an elevation of 6,000 feet

evidence.claim: The original toll was five dollars for each wagon.
evidence.quote: specified toll rates at five dollars (about a week's wages, equivalent to about $179.00 today) for each wagon

evidence.claim: A better road was blasted through the hill in 1861, ending the route’s effectively one-way passage.
evidence.quote: The direction of travel was effectively one-way until 1861, when a better road was blasted through Laurel Hill.

evidence.claim: Government Camp also has a smaller ski area of its own, Summit Pass.
evidence.quote: Government Camp also has its own, smaller ski resort, Summit Pass.

evidence.claim: Fireplace screens were made from tire chains, and railroad tracks supplied metal for the ironwork.
evidence.quote: Fireplace screens were fashioned from tire chains. Andirons and other iron work were forged from railroad tracks.
